paras: The attempted lynching of Archie Hill was a mob's effort to lynch a Black man in Pasadena, California, after he was accused of fatally shooting streetcar conductor Will Carlton in a fare dispute at the end of May or start of June 1903. Hill was lodged in the Los Angeles county jail, and according to the Sedalia Times the 'hoodlum element' of Pasadena then turned on the city's Black residents. Hill was later convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life, an outcome white papers in Kansas and Colorado reported as hometown news about Carlton without any mention of a mob.

Carlton, born in Wichita, Kansas, about twenty-five years earlier, had worked for the Santa Fe railroad before becoming a conductor on the Pacific Railway Company's Pasadena line, wearing badge No. 128.

According to the Pasadena News, as reprinted in the Wichita Daily Eagle, Hill boarded Carlton's car at 8 o'clock on a Sunday night at Fair Oaks avenue and Colorado street and, after paying his fare, claimed he had handed over a $5 gold piece and demanded $4.95 in change. Carlton refused, and Hill left the car at Marengo avenue, met it again at Worcester avenue and renewed his demand. In the News account Hill then drew a .38-calibre revolver and shot Carlton in the stomach 'without a word of warning', and the weapon misfired twice more. Hill ran, stumbled and was seized by Policeman John O. Reynolds, who handcuffed him and took him to the city jail.

The Sedalia Times, relying on 'the colored man's statement', said the conductor had kept the change from a $5 gold piece and that a fight preceded the shooting. Carlton died the following Thursday. The same paper reported that 'an attempt was made to lynch the colored man' but that he was safely lodged in the Los Angeles county jail; it gave no details of the crowd, its leaders or when it gathered.

After the attempt failed, the Sedalia Times wrote, the 'hoodlum element of Pasadena' set out to avenge themselves by insulting every Black person in the city, and a petition circulated asking restaurant keepers to refuse accommodations to all Black people. The paper added that 'better judgment prevailed' and predicted a return to normal conditions. No report of arrests or charges against the would-be lynchers appears in the coverage.

In October 1903 Hill was found guilty of murder in the first degree and sentenced to life imprisonment at hard labor, news that reached Carlton's brother Rufus in Wichita by message. The La Junta Tribune reported that Hill admitted at trial he had given Carlton only a five-cent piece, and that he claimed to be an illegitimate son of Senator Ben Hill of Georgia.

The only Black-press report found ran on June 13 in the Sedalia Times, a Missouri weekly, as a brief among items of race news. It opened with Hill's own account of the dispute, called him 'a Negro' and 'the colored man', and placed the blame for the aftermath on Pasadena's 'hoodlum element'.

The white coverage came from towns with ties to the dead man: the Wichita Daily Eagle ran 'Death of Will Carlton' on June 23 and 'Murderer Given Life Sentence' on October 28, and the La Junta Tribune ran 'Life Imprisonment' on October 24. The Eagle noted that the first telegrams said only that Carlton was 'shot by a negro', and its reprinted Pasadena News account ends with Hill's arrest and says nothing of a mob. In Vermont the St. Johnsbury Caledonian treated the case as a funeral curiosity, describing the conductor as 'mercilessly shot while on duty, by a mulatto passenger'. None of the white articles mentions the lynching attempt or the treatment of Pasadena's Black residents.

The Wichita reports place the shooting on Sunday, June 1, or May 31, while the La Junta Tribune placed it in Los Angeles in July, a date contradicted by the June reports of Carlton's death. The Pasadena News described a verbal dispute followed by a shot without warning, whereas the Sedalia Times, drawing on Hill's statement, said a fight came first.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Archie Hill
bases: The only Black-press report says a mob attempt was made to lynch Hill, who was saved by removal to the Los Angeles county jail, followed by harassment of Pasadena's Black residents (A1, A2); this is an attempted, not completed, lynching.

The shooting, arrest and conviction are corroborated by several white papers (A4, A8, A9), but the lynching attempt and the harassment that followed appear only in the Sedalia Times (A1, A2); the white accounts neither mention nor deny a mob.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Sedalia Times)
accounts.gist: By Hill's statement he gave the conductor a $5 gold piece and was refused change; a fight followed and Hill shot the conductor dead. A lynching attempt failed when Hill was lodged in the county jail, and Pasadena's 'hoodlum element' then turned on the city's Black residents.

accounts.label: Pasadena News (reprinted in Wichita Daily Eagle)
accounts.gist: Hill claimed a $5 gold piece, left the car, reboarded, renewed the dispute and shot Carlton 'without a word of warning'; he fled and was captured by Policeman Reynolds and taken to the city jail. No mob is mentioned.

accounts.label: La Junta Tribune (trial report)
accounts.gist: Hill was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life; at trial he admitted he had given only a five-cent piece.

framing.detail: The Sedalia Times led with Hill's own statement, reported the lynching attempt without detail, and condemned the 'hoodlum element of Pasadena' for insulting every Black person in the city.

The Wichita Daily Eagle ran 'Death of Will Carlton' and 'Murderer Given Life Sentence' as hometown news, reprinting the Pasadena News account, which ends with Hill's arrest and does not mention a mob.
The La Junta Tribune ('Life Imprisonment') called Hill 'the negro' throughout and stressed his trial admission that he had given only five cents.
The St. Johnsbury Caledonian's 'A Unique Floral Offering' described the conductor as 'mercilessly shot while on duty, by a mulatto passenger'.

versions.value: In Los Angeles during the month of July

conflicts.note: Both Wichita reports and the Pasadena News place the shooting on a Sunday night shortly before June 4; the La Junta 'July' is contradicted by the June reports of Carlton's death.
